title: Designing Time Series Experiments in A/B Testing with Transformer Reinforcement Learning
claim: Encode the full history with a sequence encoder into states, then let an RL agent optimize allocation against an error objective in a closed loop.
layout: Single row, left-to-right, with a bottom feedback loop and MSE arrows
description: A single wide left-to-right pipeline diagram. At the far left are three rows of colored circular tokens: orange O, red A, green Y, and gray [PAD] tokens, which show variable-length history sequences padded to equal length. These feed three pink boxes labeled Q, K and V, which represent a transformer encoder. The encoder outputs a dotted box of stacked state, action and reward triples, S_t in blue, A_t in red and R_t in pink. Black arrows labeled MSE loop from the top and bottom of the input sequences back to this box. The states then go into a second dotted box showing a Double DQN, with purple and cyan neural-network node graphs labeled Target Network and Q-Network. An arrow leads to the text 'Optimal Design'. A return arrow passes through a globe icon labeled 'Simulation Environment' and back to the inputs, which closes the loop. The eye starts at the colorful token rows.
caption: Illustration of the proposed transformer reinforcement learning algorithm. Our algorithm employs a transformer encoder to summarize the full historical context and to produce the state {St}t. These states are then fed into a double deep Q-network agent, which outputs an optimal policy that minimizes the mean squared error of the ATE estimator (encoded as the (negative) reward {Rt}t).
abstract: A/B testing has become a gold standard for modern technological companies to conduct policy evaluation. Yet, its application to time series experiments, where policies are sequentially assigned over time, remains challenging. Existing designs suffer from two limitations: (i) they do not fully leverage the entire history for treatment allocation; (ii) they rely on strong assumptions to approximate the objective function (e.g., the mean squared error of the estimated treatment effect) for optimizing the design. We first establish an impossibility theorem showing that failure to condition on the full history leads to suboptimal designs, due to the dynamic dependencies in time series experiments. To address both limitations simultaneously, we next propose a transformer reinforcement learning (RL) approach which leverages transformers to condition allocation on the entire history and employs RL to directly optimize the MSE without relying on restrictive assumptions. Empirical evaluations on synthetic data, a publicly available dispatch simulator, and a real-world ridesharing dataset demonstrate that our proposal consistently outperforms existing designs.
